## Back to Nogales

We want to test our theory of development: $X \Rightarrow Y$ 

![](figures/nogales.png){width="50%" fig-align="center"}


::: {.fragment .fade-in}
This requires a though experiment: without some factor ($X$), N (US) would have been like N (MX)
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Central to the though experiment is the [counterfactual]{.alert} (what if...)
:::


## Testing Theories in Comparative Politics

Comparativists formulate and test theories of politics

- Theories typically contain causal statements: $X \Rightarrow Y$
    - "Changing $X$ causes a change in $Y$"
- Test a causal theory $\rightarrow$ "does the relationship hold in the data?"
- Key issue: when $X$ changes also $Z$ changes. Which one caused $Y$?
- Without *holding* $Z$ *constant* we cannot know if $X \Rightarrow Y$

. . . 

Causal inference is the main methodology

- Traditionally there were other tools (case study, controlled comparison)
- Today statistical methods are mainstream $\rightarrow$ [control]{.alert} for several $Z$

---

# Basics of Causal Inference {.section}

## Causal Research Questions

We start by formulating a hypothesis, derived from a theory 

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

::: {style="text-align: center"}
Majoritarian electoral systems reduce taxation
:::


<div style="height: 1em;"></div>


::: {.fragment .fade-in}
This hypothesis is causal. It says that MAJ cause the level of taxation.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
It implies two [counterfactual]{.alert} states of the world

- Countries with MAJ would have higher tax rate if they did not have MAJ
- Countries without MAJ would have lower tax rate if they had MAJ
::: 




## Causal Effects

Consider a country under two different counterfactual conditions:


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "620px"
#| out-height: "290px"

library(grid)

grid.newpage()

# Create viewport
pushViewport(viewport(width = 1, height = 1))

# Left square - Untreated state
grid.rect(x = 0.25, y = 0.55, width = 0.35, height = 0.5, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "gray90", col = "black", lwd = 4))
grid.text("Country\n(Untreated)", x = 0.25, y = 0.2, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 28))

# Right square - Treated state  
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.55, width = 0.35, height = 0.5, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "gray90", col = "black", lwd = 4))
grid.text("Country\n(Treated)", x = 0.75, y = 0.2, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 28))

# Stylized ballot box in the treated state (Majoritarian System)
# Ballot box body
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.48, width = 0.16, height = 0.20, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "lightblue", col = "black", lwd = 3))
# Ballot box lid
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.585, width = 0.18, height = 0.03, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "skyblue3", col = "black", lwd = 2.5))
# Slot on lid
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.585, width = 0.08, height = 0.008, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "black"))
# Ballot paper inserted into slot
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.65, width = 0.09, height = 0.11, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "white", col = "black", lwd = 2))
# Checkmark on ballot
grid.lines(x = c(0.725, 0.745, 0.775), y = c(0.65, 0.63, 0.68), 
           gp = gpar(col = "darkgreen", lwd = 3.5, lineend = "round"))
# "MAJ" label on ballot box
grid.text("MAJ", x = 0.75, y = 0.47, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 20, fontface = "bold", col = "navy"))

# Label for counterfactual states
grid.text("Two Counterfactual States", x = 0.5, y = 0.05, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 30, fontface = "bold"))

popViewport()
```


:::{.fragment}
The **only difference** between the two conditions is the **treatment** (MAJ or not), everything else is the same
:::

$Y$ is the outcome variable (e.g., tax rate, tax revenue as % of GDP)


::: {.fragment}
[Unit treatment effect]{.alert} (UTE) = difference in country's $Y$ between the two conditions 

[Average treatment effect]{.alert} (ATE) = average of the UTE for all countries
:::



## Causality and Counterfactuals

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "620px"
#| out-height: "290px"

library(grid)

grid.newpage()

# Create viewport
pushViewport(viewport(width = 1, height = 1))

# Left square - Untreated state (DASHED - unobserved)
grid.text("UNOBSERVED", x = 0.25, y = 0.88,

grid.rect(x = 0.25, y = 0.55, width = 0.35, height = 0.5, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "gray90", col = "black", lwd = 4, lty = "dashed"))
grid.text("Country\n(Untreated)", x = 0.25, y = 0.2, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 28))

# Right square - Treated state (SOLID - observed)
grid.text("OBSERVED", x = 0.75, y = 0.88, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 20, col = "darkgreen", fontface = "italic"))
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.55, width = 0.35, height = 0.5, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "gray90", col = "black", lwd = 4))
grid.text("Country\n(Treated)", x = 0.75, y = 0.2, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 28))

# Stylized ballot box in the treated state (Majoritarian System)
# Ballot box body
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.48, width = 0.16, height = 0.20, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "lightblue", col = "black", lwd = 3))
# Ballot box lid
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.585, width = 0.18, height = 0.03, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "skyblue3", col = "black", lwd = 2.5))
# Slot on lid
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.585, width = 0.08, height = 0.008, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "black"))
# Ballot paper inserted into slot
grid.rect(x = 0.75, y = 0.65, width = 0.09, height = 0.11, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "white", col = "black", lwd = 2))
# Checkmark on ballot
grid.lines(x = c(0.725, 0.745, 0.775), y = c(0.65, 0.63, 0.68), 
           gp = gpar(col = "darkgreen", lwd = 3.5, lineend = "round"))
# "MAJ" label on ballot box
grid.text("MAJ", x = 0.75, y = 0.47, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 20, fontface = "bold", col = "navy"))

# Label for counterfactual states
grid.text("Two Counterfactual States", x = 0.5, y = 0.05, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 30, fontface = "bold"))

popViewport()
```

The problem is that a country either has an ES or it has another. It can't have both together. This is the [fundamental problem of causal inference]{.alert}

. . . 

::: {.callout-important title="The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference"}
We cannot observe the same unit under two conditions, so the unit treatment effect cannot be observed
:::



## Average Treatment Effects

Suppose electoral systems (treatment) are allocated **randomly** to countries

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: "650px"
#| out-height: "290px"

library(grid)

grid.newpage()

# Create viewport
pushViewport(viewport(width = 1, height = 1))

# Define positions for 4 countries (2x2 grid)
positions <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.25, 0.75, 0.25, 0.75),
  y = c(0.65, 0.65, 0.35, 0.35),
  treated = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)  # Countries 2 and 3 are treated
)

# Draw all 4 countries
for (i in 1:4) {
  # Draw rectangle (all solid borders)
  grid.rect(x = positions$x[i], y = positions$y[i], 
            width = 0.3, height = 0.22, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "gray90", col = "black", lwd = 3))
  
  # Add stylized ballot box for treated countries (Majoritarian System)
  if (positions$treated[i]) {
    # Ballot box body
    grid.rect(x = positions$x[i], y = positions$y[i] - 0.02, 
              width = 0.09, height = 0.10, 
              gp = gpar(fill = "lightblue", col = "black", lwd = 2))
    # Ballot box lid
    grid.rect(x = positions$x[i], y = positions$y[i] + 0.035, 
              width = 0.10, height = 0.016, 
              gp = gpar(fill = "skyblue3", col = "black", lwd = 1.5))
    # Slot on lid
    grid.rect(x = positions$x[i], y = positions$y[i] + 0.035, 
              width = 0.045, height = 0.004, 
              gp = gpar(fill = "black"))
    # Ballot paper inserted into slot
    grid.rect(x = positions$x[i], y = positions$y[i] + 0.065, 
              width = 0.05, height = 0.055, 
              gp = gpar(fill = "white", col = "black", lwd = 1.2))
    # Checkmark on ballot
    grid.lines(x = c(positions$x[i] - 0.012, positions$x[i] - 0.002, positions$x[i] + 0.014), 
               y = c(positions$y[i] + 0.065, positions$y[i] + 0.055, positions$y[i] + 0.08), 
               gp = gpar(col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2, lineend = "round"))
    # "MAJ" label on ballot box
    grid.text("MAJ", x = positions$x[i], y = positions$y[i] - 0.025, 
              gp = gpar(fontsize = 11, fontface = "bold", col = "navy"))
  }
}

# Label at bottom
grid.text("Sample of Countries with Majoritarian System Allocated", 
          x = 0.5, y = 0.05, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 24, fontface = "bold"))

popViewport()
```

- Countries with MAJ $\rightarrow$ treatment group
- Countries without MAJ $\rightarrow$ control group

::: {.fragment}
$\implies$ Random assignment allows to identify the ATE 
:::

## The Benefits of Randomization

$\implies$ Random assignment allows to identify the ATE 


::: {.fragment}
Key intuition: random assignment is "blind" to any differences between units. *On average*, the control group is very similar to the treated group if it were not treated
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

- Example 1: students' height 
- Example 2: testing drug pill in hospital 

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

::: {.fragment}
$\implies$ In causal inference, we typically focus on the ATE.
:::



## Estimate an Effect Under Random Assignment

If electoral systems were randomized across countries, we could simply compare the average $Y$ between the treated and control group.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-height: "200px"    # <--- Forces display size
#| out-width: "auto"      # <--- Maintains aspect ratio
#| 
library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# Create a simple DAG without confounding
dag <- dagify(
  Y ~ D,
  coords = list(x = c(D = 1, Y = 3),
                y = c(D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Causal effect: D → Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

:::
::: {.column widt="50%}
We can do this with a *linear regression*.


$Y = \alpha + \beta D + \varepsilon$

- $Y$ = taxation outcome (e.g., tax rate)
- $D$ = variable that indicates whether a country has MAJ (1=yes, 0=no)
- $\beta$ = estimate of the ATE

:::
::::

## When We Can't Run an Experiment

To estimate the ATE of $X$ on $Y$ we need to randomly change $X$ 

- Scientists conduct [randomized experiments]{.alert} 
- In political science, randomization often unfeasible or unethical
- In these cases, we look at events that have already happened 
    - Use observational data and look for [natural experiments]{.alert}

. . . 

We then need [identification assumptions]{.alert} about the "randomness"

- E.g., assume the electoral system was somehow chosen by chance
- We can do causal inference only if these assumptions are very plausible
- This depends on our *knowledge* of the assignment process 


## The Problem of Endogeneity

Imagine that countries adopt electoral institutions based on economic conditions: richer countries are more likely to adopt MAJ

. . . 

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-height: "400px"    # <--- Forces display size
#| out-width: "auto"      # <--- Maintains aspect ratio

library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# Create a DAG with confounding
dag_confounded <- dagify(
  Y ~ D + Income,
  D ~ Income,
  coords = list(x = c(Income = 2, D = 1, Y = 3),
                y = c(Income = 2, D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_confounded, node_size = 20) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Income (confounder) affects both D and Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

If we simply compare treated and non-treated countries as before, and run $Y = \alpha + \beta D + \varepsilon$, we will get:

$$\beta= \text{ATE}$$
$$+ \underbrace{\text{prior income differences}}_{\text{bias}}$$

:::

::::

. . . 

We call this [selection]{.alert} or [endogeneity]{.alert} or [confounding]{.alert} or [omitted variable]{.alert}.

. . . 

$\implies$ "correlation is not causation"


## Address Endogeneity

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-height: "400px"    
#| out-width: "auto"      

library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# Create a DAG with confounding
dag_confounded <- dagify(
  Y ~ D + Income,
  D ~ Income,
  coords = list(x = c(Income = 2, D = 1, Y = 3),
                y = c(Income = 2, D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_confounded, node_size = 20) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Income affects both D and Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
If we include income in a multivariate regression, we "keep it constant" and compare units with the same income

$Y = \alpha + \beta D + \gamma \text{Income} + \varepsilon$

and now 

$\beta=\text{ATE}$

:::

::::

## Common Forms of Endogeneity

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-height: "380px"
#| out-width: "auto"

library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# DAG 1: Confounding with generic confounder
dag_confounding <- dagify(
  Y ~ D + C,
  D ~ C,
  coords = list(x = c(C = 2, D = 1, Y = 3),
                y = c(C = 2, D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_confounding, node_size = 20) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Common Cause") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-height: "380px"
#| out-width: "auto"

library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# DAG 2: Reverse causality
dag_reverse <- dagify(
  D ~ Y,
  coords = list(x = c(D = 1, Y = 3),
                y = c(D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_reverse, node_size = 20) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Reverse Causality") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 16, face = "bold"))
```

:::

::::



## We Need a Causal Research Design

To recap: we want to test a theory that says $X \Rightarrow Y$

- Find a setting where $X$ can be thought of as random 
- Background knowledge on how $X$ was determined
- If not random, we need to remove the source of endogeneity 
- Use statistical methods to estimate ATE

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

. . . 

[Causal Research Design]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ select units, comparisons, methods to estimate ATE in a credible way


## From Between-Country to Within-Country

Common solution: using within-country units reduces endogeneity issues

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: "680px"
#| out-height: "290px"

library(grid)

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(width = 1, height = 1))

# Helper function to draw a mini ballot box
draw_ballot_box <- function(xc, yc) {
  # Body
  grid.rect(x = xc, y = yc - 0.015, width = 0.05, height = 0.055, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "lightblue", col = "black", lwd = 1.2))
  # Lid
  grid.rect(x = xc, y = yc + 0.015, width = 0.058, height = 0.01, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "skyblue3", col = "black", lwd = 1))
  # Slot
  grid.rect(x = xc, y = yc + 0.015, width = 0.025, height = 0.003, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "black"))
  # Ballot paper
  grid.rect(x = xc, y = yc + 0.033, width = 0.028, height = 0.032, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "white", col = "black", lwd = 0.8))
  # Checkmark
  grid.lines(x = c(xc - 0.007, xc - 0.001, xc + 0.008), 
             y = c(yc + 0.033, yc + 0.027, yc + 0.042), 
             gp = gpar(col = "darkgreen", lwd = 1.5, lineend = "round"))
  # Text
  grid.text("MAJ", x = xc, y = yc - 0.018, 
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 7, fontface = "bold", col = "navy"))
}

# ================= LEFT: Between-Country Comparison =================
grid.text("Between-Country Comparison", x = 0.24, y = 0.92, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 18, fontface = "bold"))

# Positions for 4 countries
cntry_pos <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.14, 0.34, 0.14, 0.34),
  y = c(0.68, 0.68, 0.40, 0.40),
  treated = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE),
  label = c("Country A", "Country B", "Country C", "Country D")
)

for (i in 1:4) {
  grid.rect(x = cntry_pos$x[i], y = cntry_pos$y[i], width = 0.16, height = 0.20, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "gray90", col = "black", lwd = 2))
  grid.text(cntry_pos$label[i], x = cntry_pos$x[i], y = cntry_pos$y[i] - 0.07, 
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"))
  if (cntry_pos$treated[i]) {
    draw_ballot_box(cntry_pos$x[i], cntry_pos$y[i] + 0.02)
  }
}

grid.text("Cross-national confounders\n(different institutions, history, culture)", 
          x = 0.24, y = 0.18, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 12, fontface = "italic", col = "firebrick"))

# ================= CENTER: Arrow =================
grid.lines(x = c(0.44, 0.51), y = c(0.54, 0.54), 
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.35, "cm"), type = "closed"), 
           gp = gpar(fill = "navy", col = "navy", lwd = 3))
grid.text("Hold national\nfactors constant", x = 0.475, y = 0.63, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold", col = "navy"))

# ================= RIGHT: Within-Country Comparison =================
grid.text("Within-Country Comparison", x = 0.76, y = 0.92, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 18, fontface = "bold"))

# Outer Country Box
grid.rect(x = 0.76, y = 0.54, width = 0.42, height = 0.54, 
          gp = gpar(fill = "aliceblue", col = "royalblue4", lwd = 3))
grid.text("Same Outer Country (National context held constant)", 
          x = 0.76, y = 0.77, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 12, fontface = "bold", col = "royalblue4"))

# Positions for 4 municipalities inside the outer country
muni_pos <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.66, 0.86, 0.66, 0.86),
  y = c(0.62, 0.62, 0.40, 0.40),
  treated = c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE),
  label = c("Municipality 1", "Municipality 2", "Municipality 3", "Municipality 4")
)

for (i in 1:4) {
  grid.rect(x = muni_pos$x[i], y = muni_pos$y[i], width = 0.15, height = 0.17, 
            gp = gpar(fill = "gray92", col = "black", lwd = 1.5))
  grid.text(muni_pos$label[i], x = muni_pos$x[i], y = muni_pos$y[i] - 0.058, 
            gp = gpar(fontsize = 9, fontface = "bold"))
  if (muni_pos$treated[i]) {
    draw_ballot_box(muni_pos$x[i], muni_pos$y[i] + 0.02)
  }
}

grid.text("Higher internal validity\n(shared national institutions & context)", 
          x = 0.76, y = 0.18, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 12, fontface = "italic", col = "darkgreen"))

# Bottom Title
grid.text("Comparing subnational units within the same country improves internal validity", 
          x = 0.5, y = 0.05, 
          gp = gpar(fontsize = 15, fontface = "bold"))

popViewport()
```

. . .

However, this may change the scope of the theory or the relevance

- Civil wars are by definition country-specific
- Within country we can compare specific elements of the same war

# Causal Research Designs {.section}

## Randomized Experiments

The "gold standard" of causal inference

- **Field experiments**. Treatment administration and outcome measurement in the real world.
    - Widely used in political science and economics
    - E.g., randomize vote encouragement letters to study the effects on turnout

- **Survey experiments**. Treatment administration and outcome measurement within a survey.
    - Longer tradition in political science to study public opinion
    - E.g., randomize how information is presented to study the effects on voters' opinion  
    - Measures psychological mechanisms rather than real-world effects


## Control Variables

Endogeneity is due to known variables in the data

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-height: "400px"    
#| out-width: "auto"      
#| 
library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# Create a DAG with confounding
dag_confounded <- dagify(
  Y ~ D + C,
  D ~ C,
  coords = list(x = c(C = 2, D = 1, Y = 3),
                y = c(C = 2, D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_confounded, node_size = 20) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "C causes D and Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

Run multivariate regression that includes the confounder as a control variables

$Y = \alpha + \beta D + \gamma \text{(control variables)} + \varepsilon$

:::

::::

## Instrumental Variables

Endogeneity is due to unobserved variables (we cannot control), but "part" of the treatment is caused by a random variable

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-height: "300px"    
#| out-width: "auto"      
#| 
library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# Create an IV DAG
dag_iv <- dagify(
  Y ~ D + C,
  D ~ Z + C,
  coords = list(x = c(Z = 1, C = 2.5, D = 2, Y = 4),
                y = c(Z = 2, C = 3, D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_iv) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Z causes D, D causes Y, but Z does not directly cause Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12))
```

The [instrumental variable]{.alert} $\rightarrow$ exogenous/random and has a causal effect on the treatment ($\approx$ a random "push" to accept)


## Instrumental Variables

Endogeneity is due to unobserved variables (we cannot control), but "part" of the treatment is caused by a random variable

:::: {.columns}


::: {.column width = "50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-height: "400px"    
#| out-width: "auto"      
#| 
library(ggdag)
library(ggplot2)

# Create an IV DAG
dag_iv <- dagify(
  Y ~ D + C,
  D ~ Z + C,
  coords = list(x = c(Z = 1, C = 2.5, D = 2, Y = 4),
                y = c(Z = 2, C = 3, D = 1, Y = 1))
)

ggdag(dag_iv) +
  theme_dag_blank() +
  labs(title = "Z causes D, D causes Y, but Z does not directly cause Y") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 12))
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

First stage: $D = \delta + \theta Z + u$

Second stage: $Y = \alpha + \beta D + \varepsilon$

:::

::::

The statistical model estimates the "first stage", then predicts the values of $D$ and replaces $D$ wiht them in the "second stage"

::: {.fragment}
$\implies$ same as controlling for the "endogenous part" of $D$ 
:::



## Difference-in-Differences

Treatment happens in time only for some units

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "750px"
#| out-height: "350px"

library(ggplot2)

did_data <- data.frame(
  group = factor(rep(c("Control", "Treated"), each = 2), levels = c("Control", "Treated")),
  time = factor(rep(c("Before", "After"), 2), levels = c("Before", "After")),
  outcome = c(4.0, 5.5, 5.0, 8.5)
)

counterfactual_data <- data.frame(
  group = "Treated (Counterfactual)",
  time = factor(c("Before", "After"), levels = c("Before", "After")),
  outcome = c(5.0, 6.5)
)

y_treated_post <- 8.5
y_cf_post <- 6.5

ggplot() +
  # Vertical treatment timing line
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 9.2, label = "Treatment Intervention", 
           color = "grey40", size = 3.8, fontface = "italic") +
  # Counterfactual line & points
  geom_line(data = counterfactual_data, aes(x = as.numeric(time), y = outcome), 
            linetype = "dashed", color = "#4A5568", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = counterfactual_data, aes(x = as.numeric(time), y = outcome), 
             color = "#4A5568", size = 3, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 1.5) +
  # Observed lines & points
  geom_line(data = did_data, aes(x = as.numeric(time), y = outcome, color = group), 
            linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = did_data, aes(x = as.numeric(time), y = outcome, color = group), 
             size = 4) +
  # Bracket for ATT
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2.08, xend = 2.08, y = y_cf_post, yend = y_treated_post), 
               color = "#C53030", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2.04, xend = 2.08, y = y_cf_post, yend = y_cf_post), 
               color = "#C53030", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2.04, xend = 2.08, y = y_treated_post, yend = y_treated_post), 
               color = "#C53030", linewidth = 1.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.12, y = (y_cf_post + y_treated_post) / 2, 
           label = "Treatment Effect\n(ATE [ATT])", color = "#C53030", size = 4.2, 
           fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, lineheight = 0.95) +
  # Annotations for parallel counterfactual
  annotate("text", x = 2.05, y = y_cf_post - 0.35, label = "Counterfactual\n(Parallel Trend)", 
           color = "#4A5568", size = 3.3, fontface = "italic", hjust = 0, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), labels = c("Before", "After"), limits = c(0.8, 2.5)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control" = "#718096", "Treated" = "#2B6CB0")) +
  labs(x = "Time Period", y = "Outcome (Y)", color = "Group") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 20)
  )
```

. . . 

We compare changes between treated units and untreated units

. . .

The assumption is [parallel trends]{.alert} in absence of treatment


## Regression Discontinuity Design 

Treatment is applied only/more to units on one side of a cutoff value

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "750px"
#| out-height: "350px"

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
n_pts <- 120
x_vals <- runif(n_pts, -3, 3)

# Outcome with a jump at x = 0
y_vals <- ifelse(
  x_vals < 0,
  3.0 + 0.6 * x_vals + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.45),
  5.8 + 0.6 * x_vals + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.45)
)

rdd_df <- data.frame(
  x = x_vals,
  y = y_vals,
  group = ifelse(x_vals < 0, "Control (Below Cutoff)", "Treated (Above Cutoff)")
)

bandwidth <- 1.2
y_control_cutoff <- 3.0
y_treated_cutoff <- 5.8

ggplot(rdd_df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = group)) +
  # Bandwidth shaded window
  annotate("rect", xmin = -bandwidth, xmax = bandwidth, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, 
           fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.35) +
  # Bandwidth boundary lines
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-bandwidth, bandwidth), linetype = "dashed", 
             color = "#4A5568", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = -bandwidth, y = 7.6, label = "- Bandwidth (h)", 
             color = "#4A5568", size = 3.3, fontface = "italic", hjust = 1.05) +
  annotate("text", x = bandwidth, y = 7.6, label = "+ Bandwidth (h)", 
             color = "#4A5568", size = 3.3, fontface = "italic", hjust = -0.05) +
  # Cutoff line
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", color = "black", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 8.0, label = "Cutoff (c = 0)", 
           color = "black", size = 3.8, fontface = "bold", vjust = -0.3) +
  # Scatter points (data points showing the discontinuity)
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 2.5) +
  # Discontinuity Jump Bracket at Cutoff
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.08, xend = 0.08, y = y_control_cutoff, yend = y_treated_cutoff), 
               color = "#C53030", linewidth = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.02, xend = 0.08, y = y_control_cutoff, yend = y_control_cutoff), 
               color = "#C53030", linewidth = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0.02, xend = 0.08, y = y_treated_cutoff, yend = y_treated_cutoff), 
               color = "#C53030", linewidth = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.15, y = (y_control_cutoff + y_treated_cutoff) / 2, 
           label = "Causal Jump\n(Local Effect / LATE)", color = "#C53030", size = 4.0, 
           fontface = "bold", hjust = 0, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Control (Below Cutoff)" = "#718096", 
                                "Treated (Above Cutoff)" = "#2B6CB0")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-3.2, 3.2), breaks = seq(-3, 3, by = 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Running Variable (Distance to Cutoff)",
    y = "Outcome (Y)",
    color = "Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 20, 10, 20)
  )
```

. . .

We compare units very close to the cutoff, that are arguably very similar

. . . 

The assumption is that they cannot alter their score to be on the other side


# Summing up {.section}

## What We Learned Today

- Testing theories means testing causal relationships
- The Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference is the key problem
- Randomization partially solves it $\rightarrow$ average effects
- Ideally we would always run randomized experiments
- Hardly feasible in political science
- We want to study real-world (observational) data with a causal research design
- We must understand the process of treatment assignment
- Different designs estimate effects under some assumptions
